source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Online experiment testing whether the ACH matrix layout reduces confirmation bias. The ACH-style matrix (hypotheses in columns, evidence in rows) did not help. A reversed layout (hypotheses in rows, evidence in columns) did.
numbers: Study 1 N=161. Task 1 chose the confirmation-consistent Hypothesis-A: HypCol (ACH style) 61.8% (34 of 55); HypRow 39.2% (20 of 51); HypText (paragraph) 67.3% (37 of 55). HypRow differed from chance (p=0.003); HypCol p=0.327; HypText p=0.048.
limits: Single scenario; online sample; the one layout that worked is not what ACH prescribes. Layout effect, not the 'consider all hypotheses' principle.
agent_relevance: Layout of evidence can change bias; copying the ACH matrix verbatim is not enough. Test layout (rows=hypotheses) in the scaffold.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: The ACH-style matrix did not make people more sensitive to source credibility.
numbers: Sensitivity to credibility (switch to Hypothesis-B in Task 3B after A in 3A): HypCol 77%, HypRow 78%, HypText 75%. No condition difference.
limits: Credibility test was one task item.
agent_relevance: A matrix does not by itself force re-weighting when evidence reliability changes. Add an explicit re-weight step when a source is discredited.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Study 2: most Dutch military analysts did not show confirmation bias on the same task. So the premise behind ACH (analysts are biased) is weaker than assumed.
numbers: Study 2 N=62 analysts. 66.1% used a balanced (BAL) strategy, 14.5% inconsistent-only (INCONS); the rest (about 19%, derived by subtraction) used consistent-only (CONS). 98% of BAL users were sensitive to credibility vs 72.7% of CONS users.
limits: One national sample, 80% male, mean age 32; lab vignette.
agent_relevance: Expert baseline is already decent; SAT gains must be shown against expert baselines. Same for LLM baselines: measure the bias first.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Neither logical coherence (additivity of probabilities) nor cognitive reflection (CRT) separated better from worse hypothesis evaluators.
numbers: Correlations between CRT score and mean absolute deviation from additivity were reported per condition; none predicted performance.
limits: Limited power; CRT is a crude trait measure.
agent_relevance: Reflection ability does not predict who benefits; gating techniques by individual difference is not supported.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Summary of earlier ACH experiments with analysts and students: ACH may not reduce bias and may raise error. In the cited analyst study about 80% of controls spontaneously rebuilt an ACH-style matrix; only about a third of ACH-trained law students used the matrix and rated it 57/100 helpful.
numbers: 80% of control group built a matrix themselves (Dhami et al. 2019, as cited); one third of trained students used it; helpfulness 57 of 100 (Maegherman et al. 2020, as cited).
limits: Secondhand figures as reported in the 2024 paper; not checked against originals.
agent_relevance: Control groups often do the technique anyway, which erases the technique effect. Check the plain baseline for already-structured behaviour.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Post-task analysis (Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami 2018, as cited) found ACH may reduce the logical coherence of probability judgments and raise error in both mean absolute error and rank order of hypotheses.
numbers: Directional claim only; the 2024 paper gives no figures for it.
limits: Secondhand; see the 2018 JDM paper for numbers.
agent_relevance: ACH-style consistency scoring can add incoherence; check probability sums in any matrix our agent builds.

source: Otzipka and Volbert (2026) The analysis of competing hypotheses and expert witness testimony: Counteracting adversarial allegiance in witness credibility assessments
finding: ACH failed to reduce adversarial allegiance (bias toward the side that hired you) in mock expert witnesses assessing a child abuse case.
numbers: N=159 with prior credibility-assessment knowledge; 3 retaining parties (defense, accessory prosecution, court) x ACH vs standard method. ACH effect on Evidence Score: F(1,153)=1.79, p=.183, partial eta2=.012. Retaining party effect: F(2,153)=3.12, p=.047, partial eta2=.039.
limits: Online vignette; the control group already used a hypothesis-testing standard approach, so the contrast is small.
agent_relevance: Role framing (who is the principal) moves judgments more than the technique. An agent told to argue one side may show the same allegiance; check this.

source: Otzipka and Volbert (2026) The analysis of competing hypotheses and expert witness testimony: Counteracting adversarial allegiance in witness credibility assessments
finding: Adversarial allegiance showed up in evidence weighting: defense-retained participants stressed evidence against credibility more than prosecution-retained ones. No difference in final credibility ratings across conditions.
numbers: Evidence Score mean difference defense vs accessory prosecution -.19, 95% CI [-.37, -.00], p=.047 (Bonferroni). Defense vs court p=.301.
limits: Borderline significance; no effect on the final rating.
agent_relevance: Bias hides in evidence selection and weighting, not in the final number. Audit the evidence step.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Argues SATs were never validated experimentally and may add noise. Heuer declined to test ACH under experimental control, relying on common sense.
numbers: Narrative review; no pooled effect size. Cites the US Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 mandating SATs.
quote: SATs actually leave a long list of implementation decisions to analysts
limits: Position paper by authors who also run the tests; cites own work.
agent_relevance: Prior for SATs should be skeptical: unvalidated tradecraft. Treat each SAT as a hypothesis to test on our own benchmark.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Reports that analysts trained in and instructed to use ACH were more susceptible to unpacking effects (incoherent probability judgments) than untrained control analysts from the same cohort.
numbers: Significant difference reported (Mandel et al. 2018); no figures in this review.
limits: Secondhand; one analyst cohort.
agent_relevance: Structured decomposition can create subadditivity. Normalize hypothesis probabilities after any matrix step.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: One-directional warnings (beware overconfidence) may only shift the response threshold, producing the mirror bias, underconfidence. Evidence of underconfidence in strategic intelligence forecasts.
numbers: Cites Mandel and Barnes 2014, 2018 and Mandel 2015; no new numbers.
limits: Hypothesis, not tested for SAT training here.
agent_relevance: An anti-overconfidence prompt may just push the agent to hedge. Measure calibration in both directions.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Inter-analyst agreement fell as source reliability and information credibility ratings (Admiralty code) became incongruent. ACH cell ratings of consistency are even less constrained.
numbers: Admiralty-code finding from Mandel (2018 annex), as cited; no figures given.
limits: Secondhand; the ACH noise claim is argued, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Noise in rubric application: fix a definition of 'consistent' (likelihood ratio) rather than leave it open.

source: Content analysis of 138 reports from IC-simulating experiments (2025) The relationship between structured analytic techniques and intelligence analysis quality (OSF preprint)
finding: Across 138 experimental reports, SATs correlated weakly with accuracy. No technique reliably predicted accuracy; the number of techniques used did not either.
numbers: 138 reports; accuracy and IC-norm adherence scores correlated weakly. Standardizing Probability Ranges and Timeline predicted norm adherence; number of unique techniques also predicted adherence.
limits: Abstract read through the OSF API only, not the full text; correlational; authors blame low power.
agent_relevance: Technique count is not a quality lever; more steps in the scaffold do not mean better answers. Favor few, tested operators.

source: Content analysis of 138 reports from IC-simulating experiments (2025) The relationship between structured analytic techniques and intelligence analysis quality (OSF preprint)
finding: SATs improved process-norm adherence (format and tradecraft standards) rather than accuracy.
numbers: Small positive correlations with adherence that 'compound' per authors.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed when read; abstract only.
agent_relevance: SATs may improve auditability, not truth. Value them for transparency, and use other mechanisms for accuracy.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: Multi-agent debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, grade-school math and chess, using 3 agents and 2 rounds.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0 / 75.0 / 81.0 / 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4 / 102.1 / 102.2 / 122.9.
limits: Same model family for all agents (ChatGPT); weaker baselines than later work; small test sets (error bars about +/-2 to 5).
agent_relevance: Original positive evidence for adversarial multi-agent use. Later work narrows it.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: Debate also improved factual accuracy. Self-reflection hurt on MMLU.
numbers: Biographies: single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9 / 57.7 / 71.1. Chess move validity 29.3 / 38.8 / 45.2.
limits: Biography task scored by a model judge.
agent_relevance: Self-critique alone can lower accuracy (MMLU 63.9 to 57.7); independent challenger agents did better than self-challenge.

source: Smit, Duckworth, Grinsztajn, et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmark of debate methods on medical and reasoning QA: debate protocols did not beat self-consistency or Medprompt out of the box.
numbers: Best-per-dataset (median in table): MedQA Medprompt 0.65, Society of Mind 0.64, Ensemble Refinement 0.64, ChatEval 0.60, Self-Consistency 0.60, single agent 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58. PubMedQA: Medprompt 0.77, single 0.75, Multi-Persona 0.70.
limits: GPT-3.5-class models of the time; hyperparameter sensitive.
agent_relevance: The devil-and-angel persona style (Multi-Persona) was the worst protocol until tuned.

source: Smit, Duckworth, Grinsztajn, et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Debate accuracy depended on how strongly agents were told to agree. Tuning the prompted agreement level turned Multi-Persona from worst to best.
numbers: With 90% prompted agreement intensity Multi-Persona beat Medprompt and Self-Consistency on MedQA (paper text: worst-performing protocol to the best-performing); exact figures are in plots only.
quote: you should agree with the other agents X% of the time
limits: Tuned on the evaluation sets; exact post-tuning accuracy not extracted from text.
agent_relevance: Dosage of dissent matters. Pure devil's advocacy (0% agreement) is not optimal; calibrate adversary strength and mix in agreement.

source: Zhang, Cui, Chen, Wang, Zhang, Wang, Wu, Hu (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Large replication-style test: 5 debate methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models (36 configurations). Debate usually failed to beat Chain-of-Thought or Self-Consistency, even with more compute.
numbers: Significant wins over CoT in only about 15% of 36 configurations (ANOVA, alpha 0.05) for SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse; Multi-Persona showed no significant gain. With GPT-4o-mini one method lost to CoT on all nine datasets. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: AgentVerse +0.85, others at least -3.60 vs CoT.
limits: Zero-shot prompts; general QA, not intelligence-type judgment.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that default adversarial debate is not a free win. Compare any red-team step with CoT and self-consistency at equal compute.

source: Zhang, Cui, Chen, Wang, Zhang, Wang, Wu, Hu (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Model heterogeneity (debaters from different model families) reliably improved debate; same-model debate did not.
numbers: Heter-SoM improved SoM-average by 6.4% and CoT-average by 5.8% (9-dataset mean); Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average.
limits: Only two-model mixes tested.
agent_relevance: If a second model is available, use it as the devil's advocate. Same-model challengers share errors.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (model re-reviews its own answer without outside feedback) does not help and often hurts. Oracle-label gains were an artifact of knowing the right answer.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round (41.8 after two). GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; HotpotQA 49, 49, 43. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5.
limits: Short-answer reasoning tasks; prompts from prior papers.
agent_relevance: Solo assumption-check or self-devil's-advocate prompts with no new evidence are risky. Challenge needs an external signal (retrieval, code, second model).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Why self-correction fails: the model cannot judge whether its reasoning is right. It more often changes correct answers to wrong than the reverse. Gains in earlier work came from weak initial prompts.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 74.7% of the time the answer was kept; of changes, correct-to-incorrect exceeded incorrect-to-correct.
limits: Only 2 rounds studied.
agent_relevance: Add a keep-unless-new-evidence rule: change an answer only if a challenge supplies new evidence.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Brainstorming comparison. Blind expert review judged LLM-generated ideas more novel than human experts' ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (1 to 10 scale; AI significant at p<0.05, Welch t, Bonferroni).
limits: Single field (NLP prompting topics); style-normalized; novelty judgment is noisy; no execution outcomes.
agent_relevance: LLMs are good at breadth in brainstorming; the bottleneck moves to selection.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: LLM brainstorming loses diversity at scale, and LLM judges cannot reliably rank ideas.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas only about 200 (5%) were non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8; duplicate rate rises with each batch. Expert judges guessed AI vs human at 50% after style normalization.
limits: Embedding similarity threshold chosen by hand inspection.
agent_relevance: Do not brainstorm by repeated sampling alone; force diversity (different frames, anti-duplication memory) and use external selection.

source: Mitigating cognitive biases in clinical decision-making through multi-agent conversations using large language models (2024, JMIR Med Inform/J Med Internet Res)
finding: GPT-4 role-play team with a devil's advocate agent plus facilitator, expert and recorder corrected cognitive-bias misdiagnoses in 16 case reports.
numbers: 16 cases x 5 repeats x 3 frameworks = 240 responses. Initial diagnosis accuracy 0% (0/80). Best framework (4-C) top-2 differential accuracy 76% (61/80); versus human evaluators odds ratio 3.49, P=.002.
limits: Cases chosen because bias caused misdiagnosis (so the initial answer was wrong by design). The best framework was the one that told the senior doctor to discuss cognitive biases explicitly. No ablation isolating the devil's advocate alone found in the text read.
agent_relevance: Most direct LLM test of a devil's advocate role; benefit looks tied to explicit bias-focused discussion, not dissent alone. A fifth agent did not participate effectively.

source: Amplifying minority voices: AI-mediated devil's advocate system (2025, IUI poster)
finding: Four-agent system (summary, conversation, duplicate checker, paraphrase) that voices private minority views as an LLM devil's advocate to improve psychological safety in group decisions.
numbers: No effect sizes found in the text read (10-page poster paper).
limits: Reliance on text-only chat and fixed intervention timing, per authors.
agent_relevance: Design pattern only; weak evidence. Not a result to rely on.
